raw_text:
### Introduction and Mechanism of Action
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health concern associated with high morbidity and mortality [1]. For decades, pharmacological management centered on suppressing the overactive renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and sympathetic nervous system. However, the introduction of the first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), sacubitril/valsartan, marked a paradigm shift [1]. Sacubitril/valsartan is a crystalline complex consisting of the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril (AHU377) and the angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) valsartan in a 1:1 molar ratio [2]. Sacubitril is metabolized to sacubitrilat, which inhibits neprilysin, an enzyme responsible for degrading vasoactive peptides like atrial and B-type natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [3]. By preventing peptide degradation, sacubitrilat promotes vasodilation, natriuresis, and inhibits cardiac fibrosis, while valsartan concurrently blocks the deleterious effects of angiotensin II on the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor [4]. Combining neprilysin inhibition with an ARB rather than an ACE inhibitor significantly reduces the risk of bradykinin-mediated angioedema [2,4].

### Morbidity and Mortality Benefits in HFrEF
The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established the clinical superiority of sacubitril/valsartan over the ACE inhibitor enalapril in chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF; left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF] ≤40%) [1]. Sacubitril/valsartan demonstrated a 20% relative risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, alongside a 16% reduction in all-cause mortality [1]. Sub-analyses revealed that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced both sudden cardiac death [5] and the risk of overall clinical progression [6]. 

### In-Hospital Initiation and Clinical Stabilization
Early clinical stabilization is crucial in acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF). The PIONEER-HF trial showed that in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan in stabilized ADHF patients was safe and led to a greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) compared to enalapril [7], alongside a significant reduction in subsequent serious clinical outcomes like rehospitalization [8]. The TRANSITION study supported these findings, demonstrating comparable safety and tolerability whether the drug was initiated in-hospital (≥12 hours pre-discharge) or shortly after discharge [9].

### Myocardial Remodeling and Functional Efficacy
Mechanistic studies have explained the clinical benefits of sacubitril/valsartan through structural cardiac changes. The PROVE-HF trial demonstrated that the reduction of NT-proBNP following sacubitril/valsartan initiation strongly correlated with significant reverse cardiac remodeling, including increased LVEF and reduced ventricular volumes [10]. Additionally, the EVALUATE-HF trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan significantly improved aortic impedance and reduced aortic stiffness [11], which can reduce ventricular afterload and improve functional mitral regurgitation [12]. However, in advanced HF (NYHA Class IV), the LIFE trial demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan did not significantly lower NT-proBNP or improve clinical outcomes compared to valsartan [13]. Conversely, pediatric clinical benefits were confirmed in the PANORAMA-HF trial, showing favorable pharmacokinetics and safety in children with systemic left ventricular systolic dysfunction [14].

### Spectrums of Ejection Fraction (HFmrEF and HFpEF)
Expanding beyond HFrEF, neprilysin inhibition was evaluated across the LVEF spectrum. Following positive Phase II data from the PARAMOUNT trial in HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF; LVEF ≥45%) [15], the Phase III PARAGON-HF trial evaluated sacubitril/valsartan against valsartan [16]. Although PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, patients reported significant improvements in quality of life [17]. Subgroup analyses highlighted substantial efficacy in women [18] and individuals with LVEF on the lower end of the preserved spectrum (45%–57%).

A pooled participant-level analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF confirmed that the clinical benefits of sacubitril/valsartan in reducing HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular mortality span a wide spectrum of LVEF, remaining robust up to an LVEF of approximately 55%–60%, with benefits extending to higher ejection fractions in women [19]. Furthermore, in patients with worsening HF and LVEF >40%, the PARAGLIDE-HF trial demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan safe initiation significantly reduced NT-proBNP [20]. A participant-level pooled analysis of PARAGLIDE-HF and PARAGON-HF confirmed that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced cardiovascular and renal events in this cohort [21]. Real-world validation from the European ARIADNE registry confirmed that starting sacubitril/valsartan in outpatient settings significantly improved real-world LVEF and functional outcomes [22].

### Renal, Metabolic, and Post-Myocardial Infarction Benefits
Sacubitril/valsartan also confers robust renal protection. In PARAGON-HF, sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced the risk of renal decline (defined as a ≥50% decrease in eGFR) compared to valsartan [23]. In the post-acute myocardial infarction setting, the PARADISE-MI trial compared sacubitril/valsartan with ramipril [24]. Although it did not meet its primary endpoint of reducing time-to-first event, subsequent analyses suggested a potential benefit in preventing total recurrent HF events post-MI [25]. Furthermore, in HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan was associated with a lower risk of severe hyperkalemia compared to enalapril, permitting safer up-titration of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) [26].

### Guidelines and Future Directions
Reflecting this vast clinical trial evidence, international guidelines establish sacubitril/valsartan as foundational. The 2021 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines recommend it as a replacement for ACE inhibitors or ARBs in HFrEF [27], and the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guidelines gave ARNI a Class I recommendation as first-line therapy [28]. The 2023 ESC Focused Update expanded these recommendations to include patients with HFmrEF and HFpEF [29]. Looking ahead, the clinical utility of sacubitril/valsartan alongside SGLT2 inhibitors continues to offer comprehensive cardiorenal protection across the full range of ejection fractions [30].
